newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Mobutu hit by fall of Kinangani.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Mobutu hit by fall of Kinangani.

text.p: Rebels captured Zaire's third city of Kisangani in the biggest setback to ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko and his government in five months of civil war.
Residents said by telephone that rebels swept almost unopposed into the city centre on Saturday after soldiers looted what they could and fled across the Zaire River.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila told a news conference at his headquarters in the eastern city of Goma that his forces did not plan to stop there.
"We are still advancing, we must liberate the whole country," he said, ruling out a ceasefire before peace negotiations.

The Tutsi-led rebels now control about one fifth of the sprawling Central African nation which Mobutu, who has rarely visited his country since undergoing prostate cancer surgery last August, has ruled since a 1965 coup.
The rebels, who are also advancing in the key southern mining province of Shaba, took up arms in October accusing the authorities of denying them citizenship.
Kabila earlier had talks with U.N. envoy Mohammed Shanoun, whose ceasefire plan the government has accepted.

Residents in Kisangani, previously the nerve centre of government military operations in the war zone, said small groups of rebels had gathered in the city centre and some people went out to welcome them.
"(Zairean soldiers) left this morning and last night after looting what they could in the short space of time that they had," one resident told Reuters by telephone.
France earlier sent a plane and 30 paratroops from a base in the Central African Republic to Kisangani and successfully airlifted out 15 foreign nationals.
Diplomats and a government official said some Zairean soldiers apparently switched sides, turning on their Serb mercenary allies at the international airport outside Kisangain.
"What happened looks distinctly like a betrayal," said a senior government official.
The diplomats spoke of heavy material damage at the airport. "There were clashes on the road from the airport when the mercenaries were trying to flee," one diplomat said.
Kabila said some of the 300 mercenaries and soldiers of Mobutu's Special Presidential Division had set up a new headquarters in Mbuji-Mayi, capital of the diamond mining province of Kasai.
The capital of Kinshasa remained calm but opposition militants in the poor district of Matonge were jubilant at news of a fresh rebel success.
"Since yesterday, we have been hearing that Kisangani is falling and here we are waiting for Kabila with our arms open," said Jose Wasunde, 34. "His army is an army of liberation."
